notes.meaning: Israel prepared to receive the land west of the Jordan River as God had promised. Three groups directed this work: Eleazar the high priest, Joshua the national leader, and the leaders of each tribe. Together they made sure the distribution was fair, honest, and done according to God's law.

The land was divided among the nine and a half tribes by casting lots. Casting lots was like drawing marked stones from an urn to let the Lord make the choice. This showed everyone that God, not human favoritism, chose where each tribe would live.

Moses had already given land east of the Jordan River to Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh. The tribe of Levi, however, did not receive a large region of land like the others. Their special work was serving God at the sanctuary, so God Himself was their portion.

The descendants of Joseph were counted as two full tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh. Because of this, there were still twelve territories to divide even though Levi received no province. Instead of farmlands, the Levites were given specific towns to live in, along with grazing fields for their animals.

The people of Israel obeyed what the Lord had commanded Moses years before. The leaders gathered to measure the land and prepare the territories for distribution. Following God's exact pattern brought order and peace to the whole nation.

Before the lots were cast, leaders from the tribe of Judah joined Caleb to approach Joshua at Gilgal. Caleb reminded Joshua of the promise God made to the two of them forty-five years earlier at Kadesh-barnea. They were the only two living men who remembered that day firsthand.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that the title Kenizzite refers to a people who originally lived outside Israel, suggesting Caleb's family was adopted into the tribe of Judah through faith.

notes.meaning: Caleb recalled being forty years old when Moses sent him out as one of twelve spies to explore Canaan. While others let fear sway them, Caleb gave an honest report based on what he truly believed. He trusted that God was far bigger than any obstacle in the land.

The other ten spies terrified the people with stories of giants and giant walls, draining Israel of all courage. Caleb stood apart from the crowd and remained completely loyal to the Lord. True faith often means standing firm even when everyone around you gives up in fear.

Because Caleb stood firm, Moses gave him a solemn oath from God that the ground he had explored would belong to him and his family forever. Wholehearted obedience brought a lasting reward. Caleb kept that promise alive in his heart through decades of waiting.

God preserved Caleb through thirty-eight years of wilderness wandering and seven years of war in Canaan. All the other adults from his generation had died in the desert, yet Caleb was now eighty-five years old and full of life. He gave God all the credit for keeping him alive.

Even at eighty-five, Caleb was just as strong and energetic as he had been at forty. He was ready for military battle as well as the daily duties of public leadership. God gave him unusual physical strength to match his spiritual endurance.

Caleb asked for the rugged hill country of Hebron, the very place guarded by fierce giants called the Anakim. He did not ask for an easy, peaceful valley, but for the toughest battleground. He humbly trusted that with God's help, he would drive the enemies out.

Joshua readily agreed to Caleb's request, gave him his blessing, and granted him Hebron as his personal inheritance. Joshua prayed for Caleb's success against the giants living there. As an old friend and leader, Joshua was glad to honor Caleb's faith.

Hebron stayed in the family of Caleb for generations because he followed the Lord God of Israel with his whole heart. His life showed that God remembers and rewards steadfast faith. Living completely for God brings blessings that outlast our own lifetime.

Before Israel took it, Hebron was known as Kiriath-arba, named after Arba, who was a legendary giant and hero among the Anakim. Caleb defeated these mighty foes, and major warfare in the land finally came to an end. God gave His people a season of peace to settle into their new homes.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the phrase about the land having rest from war was placed here by an editor to mark the end of Caleb's personal conquest after the general summary in chapter 11.
